
**Editor Comments**:
        This manuscript presents a flexible framework for estimating thermal tolerance and sensitivity, supported by extensive simulations, empirical examples, and R packages.
        
        I was excited about the manuscript during pre-assessment, particularly because this is an active field with several recent methodological advances. I felt the approach could make a timely and useful contribution.
        
        We received two thoughtful reviews, and I am grateful to both reviewers for their time and expertise. Reviewer 2 is particularly enthusiastic about the methodological rigor and practical utility of the framework, an assessment I largely share. Reviewer 1, while also recognizing these strengths, raises an important concern about novelty, particularly in relation to Bullard et al. (2026).
        
        I think this is the central issue that needs addressing. Both reviewers also offer a number of other useful suggestions for strengthening the manuscript.
        
        I therefore recommend major revision. I see considerable promise in the work, but would like the revision to focus particularly on establishing its novelty. I also intend to seek additional independent reviews of the revised manuscript to help assess this question.
        
The following reviewer comments were taken into consideration during the peer review process.

**Response**: We thank the Editor for recognising the framework's timeliness, utility and rigour. Our central methodological advance is to reparameterise dose-response models directly in terms of $CT_{max}$ and $z$, so researchers can specify and test biological hypotheses about thermal tolerance and sensitivity within a single model. $CT_{max}$ and $z$ are well engrained in the TLS literature [Rezende et al. 2014]. Indeed, these effect sizes have been used in many broad-scale comparative and meta-analytic studies [e.g., Bennet et al.; Pottier et al. etc.]. $CT_{max}$ and $z$ have a well understood biological meaning and can be used to predict survival in nature [e.g., Rezende et al. 2020]. Our re-parameterisation means that we can now fit fixed and random effects directly on these parameters allowing comparisons among species, sexes or life stages, while correctly propagating uncertainty into those inferences. Additionally, we can decompose sources of variation, such as variation among populations, families or experimental groups opening up completely new avenues for addressing fundamental questions.  Correct sampling error around $CT_{max}$ and $z$, and the ease with which it can be estimated and reported, will also improve inferences drawn from comparative meta-analytic models in the future making these studies more powerful. Our focus on the link between temperature effects on dose-response midpoints and the classical TDT relationship allows for this innovation. We believe this is a more logical way to think about connections to classical theory. Together with accessible R packages, these developments provide a practical framework for modelling the parameters of biological interest to biologists.

In our revised manuscript, we have also clarified how our contribution builds on and differs from Bullard et al. (2026). Bullard et al. (2026) identify the log-logistic scale parameter $a$ as median failure time (their Equation 1) and relate its logarithm to temperature (their Figure 2C). As indicated above, our work develops the direct $CT_{max}$ and $z$ parameterisation and its use for hierarchical inference. By allowing flexible asymptotes, we also distinguish the relative midpoint from an absolute 50% survival threshold and derive the corrections needed for $t_{50}$, $CT_{max}$ and $z$. These thresholds coincide in their log-logistic survival model, which fixes the asymptotes at 0 and 1, but such features are not characteristic of all datasets as our case studies demonstrate. Finally, our simulations evaluate bias and interval coverage across experimental designs and imposed changes in steepness and asymptotes. They assess the consequences of these changes for estimating $CT_{max}$ and $z$ and help guide experimental design. Bullard et al. (2026) did not do simulations to explore these important aspects of modelling so we add clarity about where their approach might fail.

We've worked hard in our revisions to distinguish our work from others to be clearer about our frameworks novelty.

**Reviewer 1 Comments to the Author**
 
The manuscript by Noble et al. is a nice methodological contribution that will facilitate implementation of thermal death time / thermal load sensitivity approaches. The R package appears well implemented and thoroughly documented. The documentation is a great resource for the community. My review focuses on my main concern of clarifying the relationship of the model in the manuscript to past models and justifying the differences.

**Response**: We would like to thank Reviewer 1 for their thoughtful review. We are happy to hear that they find our work to be an important methodological contribution, and its associated R packages, a "great resource for the community". We have worked hard to clarify the relationships of the 4PL model to past models and spent a bit more time justifying the differences and why we think the 4PL provides a easier model to grasp. Please also see our response to Reviewer 2's comments which hopefully will clarify these points further. We have also tried to work in to our revised manuscript the important points below as well as a broader comparison with other dose-response models. Importantly, these dose-response models work equally well, but require more adjustments. We argue that the 4PL log-logistic model is a more natural model for deriving thermal tolerance and CTmax as it's midpoint creates a more natural bridge to the TDT framework. 

It seems that a similar model (Bullard et al. 2026) was published while the authors were nearing submitting the manuscript. This manuscript cites Bullard et al. (2026) in several places but does not describe the relationship between the models. The models in the research field and their relationship are already difficult to understand and decipher, so I feel that clear describing the relationship of the manuscript's model to Bullard et al. (2026) is essential. The GitHub archive for this manuscript actually contains a solid comparison of the papers that seems to be generated by an AI LLM: https://github.com/daniel1noble/bayesTLS/commit/b27d1490b8bf680c119e3149095fc74242ee4583. I agree with the summary of the comparison:
"The honest framing: **our model is a hierarchical Bayesian generalisation of the log-logistic AFT of @bullard2026, additionally estimating asymptotes and accommodating aggregated proportion/count designs.**"

**Response**: This is partially true, but misses a fundamental point. The significance of our approach is not the specific dose-response model used. The log-logistic function is just a nice model to bridge into the TLS theory because it has nice properties and is frequently used [e.g., see Ritz et al. 2010]. Other dose-response models (Gompertz, Weibell etc) can also be used. We now show how they can be used as well in our revised manuscript. 

The significant step forward we make is the re-parameterisation of the dose-response model to allow for linear predictors on $CT_{max}$ and $z$ – the parameters that are of direct interest to biologists. Re-parameterisaton with a focus on $CT_{max}$ and $z$ completely changes modelling in the field because we can now place emphasis on the parameters that are of direct interest to us and make correct inferences about them. For example, we can model whether sexes, life stages or species differ in $CT_{max}$ and/or $z$. We can easily establish if they are significantly different or not - there is no need to use complicated workarounds to correctly propagate sampling uncertainty for inference. We can also decompose sources of variance. For example, family or clone level variance in $CT_{max}$ and $z$. None of this has been possible in previous modelling frameworks as far as we are aware. As we show in our simulations, trying to do all this through a two-stage modelling framework can go very, very wrong if not done correctly. Though, @bullard2026 also recognize that proper inference is best done in a single model, which is great.

Having said that, we agree that this point did not come across early enough or clearly enough. We have now reworked the opening introduction to make our distinction clearer. As indicated above, we have now also shown how other commonly used dose-response models can be reconceptualised in the same was as the log-logistic. We have also worked these modelling options into the bayesTLS package with the addition of new "fit_*" functions that allow users to use different dose-response models.

I briefly describe my understanding of the main differences in the approaches below:
Noble et al. add two more parameters "upper" and "lower" thresholds. The Noble et al. approach fits 4 log-logistic parameters, which are modeled across temperature (introducing more parameters) and are capable of being treated as random effects. Given the relatively small sample sizes of most relevant data to date, the model makes fitting challenging and risks overfitting. The incorporation of thresholds seems to generate some questionable fits in the supplementary examples. The thresholds are not well motivated in the manuscript and it would be helpful to compare the fit of an analogous model without the parameters to justify their inclusion and provide guidance on when thresholds are desirable. The R package is configured to enable fixing the parameters. Since most experiments start with survival of 1 at time 0, the usefulness of the additional parameters seems questionable. The authors mention accommodating “incomplete” data, but I’m not sure how much of an issue such data poses. The survival analysis literature is mature and I believe offers other statistical approaches to left censoring (upper bound) and right censoring (lower bound) data. Overall, the threshold approach should be better justified.

**Response**: We agree in principle that the additional parameters can risk overfitting, however, the model can very easily be simplified. We have made this point very clear in our discussion (LXX). Indeed, the key fit functions have a specific parameter that allows one to fix the upper and lower asymptote defaulting to a 2PL. The four parameter log-logistic was used because it is the most common model used in the dose-response literature [@ritz ] and provides maximal flexibility to accommodate different shaped functions. As we show in our simulations, if data begin to deviate in their upper, lower asymptotes or k, you can get a biased estimates of thermal tolerance and sensitivity otherwise (See section of supp). It is therefore safer to start more complex and simplify the model if needed.

We would like to remind Reviewer 1 that the actual distribution is not the main novelty of our paper. It is in fact the establishment of a clearer theoretical connection to the TDT framework and the complete re-parameterisation of the dose response curve to estimate CTmax and z in a single model. These are the parameters that are of direct interest to practitioners. The ability to propagate error to downstream analyses is also a key feature as Reviewer 1 correctly points out. To make this point clearer, we have now added this same re-paramaterisation to all relevant dose-response models in the supplement (Section), and we have worked them into bayesTLS by creating new fit_* functions. This will give opportunities to compare the fit. In many cases, random effects will not likely need to be included on all the parameters of the 4PL, particularly in the direct parameterization model formulation. These should be placed instead directly on CTmax and z, which we argue is where most people will want them anyway. Only a fixed temperature effect on 4PL parameters is necessary when one wants to calculate absolute CTmax and z, but in practice they will likely vary little with relative values. The models can therefore place temperature effects on only a subset of parameters and others can be fixed. All of this is completely flexible in bayes/freqTLS and we already make mention of this in our discussion. 

Noble et al. include the useful component of modeling uncertainty in total population survival as a binomial distribution, whereas Bullard et al. 2026 just reported the probability. The Bayesian approach in Noble et al. that enables propagating uncertainly is a methodological advance.

**Response**: Thanks! We agree. We have tried to make sure this point clearer in our revised text.

Noble et al. incorporate repair using a previously published approach (but they don't emphasize that much) whereas Bullard et al. 2026 only describe approaches for accounting for repair.

**Response**: A fair point. We did not focus on repair to avoid overcomplicating the main message of the paper. Arnold et al. (2025) already present the repair model we use, and there are excellent recent papers that model repair and, in some cases, estimate it from data (Buckley et al. 2025; Ørsted et al. 2026; Faber et al. 2026, preprint). Understanding repair is an active research area about which we still know very little. We believe it is better to show how repair can be incorporated in a simple, illustrative form until more is known, which is what we do in the heat-injury predictions (Figure 6; Methods; Supplement Section 4). We note in the Discussion that estimating repair parameters directly from experiments is a major next step (Lines 417–423 of submitted MS).

Noble et al. claim novelty in a "one stage" instead of "two stage" approach, which allows them to propagate uncertainty and changes in shape and thresholds across temperatures. Bullard et al. 2026 is also a one stage approach but they emphasize the fitting to full distributions rather than just using the mean or median survival. I find that characterization of the approach more compelling.

**Response**: We are not quite sure what Reviewer 1 means by "fitting to full distributions". We have spent some time looking at BUllard et al's (2026) code and we see now better what they have done. It is indeed a single stage model, but just the We agree in principle but it will depend on the question being asked which approach one finds more compelling. If one is interested in survival directly, yes, we agree. However, if one is interested in z and CTmax, then one needs to have z and CTmax modelled. Again, we do not think these are competing approaches but rather different derivations of common underlying survival model. 

Bullard et al. (2026) show empirically that the shape parameter changes with temperature (in violation of the assumptions of previous models). Mentioning this finding in the current manuscript could bolster the motivation for the approach. Noble et al. do include a nice validation of the approach with simulated data. Bullard et al. 2026 discuss the utility of hazard estimates in understanding responses to thermal stress, which could be useful to mention in the current manuscript.

**Response**: A good point! We agree that the shape parameter changing with temperature is important, and supports our justification for placing a temperature effect on k in the 4PL model (which we do by default). Our simulations show that this is important, adding further justification. We have now added this point to the main MS (TO DO - SENTENCE.)

Overall, the paper would be more useful if it more thoroughly describes the relationship to other modeling approaches and emphasizes areas of novelty. The manuscript and R package is a nice methodological contribution but the methodological upgrades would benefit from more justification.

**Response**: Thanks for your very helpful suggestions. We have tried to better describe the relationship to other modelling approaches, and in particular the work of Bullard et al. 2025. Please also see our response to Reviewer 2's comments about these points as well. Some are similar.
 
**Reviewer 2 Comments to the Author**
 
General comments
This paper presents a methodologically rigorous and timely contribution to thermal ecology and statistical modeling. The authors successfully address critical limitations in conventional two-stage TDT/TLS analyses by proposing a unified hierarchical four-parameter log-logistic (4PL) model. The framework elegantly avoids problems like failure to propagate uncertainty, mishandling of sparse data where survival doesn't span the full 0–1 range, and pseudoreplication issues inherent to independent temperature-by-temperature analyses. The paper's empirical validation is exceptionally strong. The simulation study systematically compares bias and 95% coverage across 29 scenario-by-design combinations totaling 29,000 simulations, demonstrating that the joint 4PL approach maintains nominal coverage (~0.95) while two-stage methods frequently collapse to values well below this threshold, especially under sparse designs and short exposure windows. The provision of two complementary R packages (bayesTLS and freqTLS) is exemplary and will substantially improve adoption across the biological community.

**Response**: Thank you for these comments. We very much appreciate the enthusiasm for our work and the very constructive feedback. We've tried to address as many points as we can within the space constraints. We believe that the comments from yourself and Reviewer 1 have really helped improve the paper. So, thanks!

Specific Comments
102-115. Model Selection and Justification. While the paper specifies the four-parameter log-logistic function clearly, there is insufficient justification for why this particular functional form was chosen over other flexible sigmoidal alternatives (e.g., Gompertz, Weibull, or other dose-response curves).
I would recommend to add a section comparing the 4PL to 2–3 competing flexible models using information criteria (AIC/BIC) or cross-validation on the empirical datasets. This would strengthen the claim that 4PL is optimal rather than convenient.

**Response**: We thank the reviewer for this comment. It also relates to important points raised by Reviewer 1. The functional form of the dose-response model is not the main contribution of this paper, but they are right to ask about this specifically. To be clear, our key contributions mainly center around: (1) the theoretical connection between a dose-response model's midpoint (or median/location) and the TDT/TLS framework (i.e., making it depend on temperature), (2) re-formalising that model so that CTmax and z become explicit linear predictors and (3) making it much easier to propagate uncertainty into any downstream inferences. As discussed above, Point 2 is particularly important because it means we can model the parameters of interest, CTmax and z, directly - understanding drivers of variance in these estimates, doing explicit variance decomposition and properly doing inference on what matters to biologists. Nonetheless, these connections work for any dose-response curve that has a parameter marking where the curve sits along the time axis (for example the log-logistic, Gompertz or Weibull curves), but it is easiest to explain for the log-logistic. We have now made this clearer in our revised manuscript (TO DO!!)

We focused on using the log-logistic for three reasons. First, its midpoint is the time by which half the responding animals have died. That is the LT50, the quantity the TDT theory is typically built on (though we show how to change that). Gompertz and Weibull curves are lopsided. Their midpoint is where the curve is steepest, at 37% or 63% mortality, not 50%. To get the LT50 line from them, the curve must first be re-written in terms of its median. The log-logistic gives it directly. In all cases, however, the midpoint is the 50% point only when mortality runs from 0% to 100%. If this isn't true, the 50% point is offset from the midpoint by an amount that depends on the asymptotes and the steepness. If the asymptotes or steepness change with temperature, so does the correction. We give these corrections in the Methods, and they are worked into bayesTLS/freqTLS. Second, although only one study, there is weak evidence the other curves fit better. For example, Bullard et al. (2026) compared the log-logistic with Weibull, log-normal and Gompertz curves on *Drosophila* failure times (11 species). In preliminary analyses the log-logistic fit as well or better by AIC (their S1 and S2 Tables). We have also now added a formal model comparison to each of our case studies that supports this point (see below). Finally, the log-logistic is the most commonly used model in the dose-response literature (e.g., see Ritz et al. 2010 review), which makes it familiar to many readers. We do not claim the log-logistic is optimal, only that it is a sensible default with the most direct link to TDT. It's midpoint is the LT50 itself, and it is the same curve conventional TDT analyses already fit at each temperature, so our model builds directly from existing practice. 

Having said that, we agree a direct comparison on our datasets would help, and we admit that we still do not yet know what model might fit best in all cases. To address this point we have done a few things. First, we have now simply integrated all the all relevant does-response models and their reformulation into `bayesTLS` re-parameterising them all. We provide a new section in the supplement describing this point and making the connections clear. Second, we now do a simple model comparison for each of our case studies comparing wAIC as a way to compare which model is best supported for each case study. We note hovered that for teh zebrasfish case study it has a sparse design. This can be problematic for distinguishing among the different models. WE THEN NEED A QUICK SUMMARY OF REULTS

384-400. Prior Specification and Sensitivity. The paper acknowledges that "Bayesian implementations require priors that are appropriate for the biological system" and that bayesTLS is "designed to make these models more accessible," but prior specifications are relegated to the supplement. The main text lacks discussion of prior sensitivity analysis.

It would be useful to include a brief section (or prominently summarize from the supplement) showing how posterior estimates of thermal sensitivity (z) and CTmax respond to plausible variations in priors. This is essential for readers to understand robustness and reproducibility.

**Response**: Good point. Prior specification was one of the main motivations for also creating the `freqTLS` R package. No priors are needed for these frequentist models and a fit with `freqTLS` can be compared to `bayesTLS` to ensure that they converge on similar answers. Nonetheless, it is worthwhile exploring prior sensitivity. We have now done that and added an explicit section in the supplement.

375-391. Model simplification guidance. The paper states that models "may at times need to be simplified, for example by ignoring temperature-dependent shifts in up, low, or k if they are not well supported by the data," but provides limited concrete guidance on when and how to apply such simplification.
I would recommend to develop a formal model selection approach (e.g., using likelihood ratio tests, AIC, or Bayesian model comparison) with worked examples showing when to retain vs. drop temperature-dependent parameters. Include a decision tree or diagnostic workflow in a figure.

**Response**: Good point. A similar point was raised by Reviewer 1 about model complexity. It is true we didn't help the reader identify when models might be overparameterised even though there are already ample facilities to help identify when simplification is warranted.

To make this clearer, we have now added a few sentences to discuss this point in teh discussions. First, as Reviewer 2 points out, different fits can be directly compared with wAIC or LOO. For example, fixing up and low and comparing it with a default model to determine if the additional estimation is warranted. Second, simplification can be justified based on effective sample sizes of posterior samples (i.e., ESS > 500), and / or chain convergence (Rhat < 1.01) of parameters in the model. Adjustments to MCMC chain length and burnin can help but if longer runs and thinning do not fix issues, we recommend simplifying models. 

282-290. Goodness-of-Fit Metrics. The paper reports realistic R2 values (e.g.,0.695[0.671–0.715] for aphids), much lower than two-stage regressions (0.97–0.996), and correctly notes this reflects fitting raw data. However, the text does not provide alternative fit summaries (e.g., Bayesian R², LOO-CV, or residual diagnostics) to aid practitioners in assessing adequacy.
It might be helpful to expand the goodness-of-fit discussion to include Bayesian R² as computed in brms, leave-one-out cross-validation metrics, and visual residual diagnostics. Show how to interpret these metrics in the context of the 4PL framework.

**Response**: We are not quite sure what Reviewer 2 means by "Bayesian R²". These are the R2 values we report already, directly from `brms`. We can definitely report LOO and residual diagnostics and we have done that now for each case study and integrated it into model validation (see our previous response).

331-334. Repair function assumptions. The repair function used in predictions is explicitly acknowledged as "illustrative and not derived empirically." While transparent, this is a substantial assumption for predictions under fluctuating temperature regimes.
It could be insightful to conduct a sensitivity analysis showing how predictions (Figure 6) change across a plausible range of repair rates and kinetics (e.g., from no repair to repair at various rates). Highlight which conclusions are robust to repair assumptions and which are not.

**Response**: Fair point. Please also see our response to Reviewer 1 in regards to this issue. In short, we did not focus on repair to avoid overcomplicating the main message of the paper. Arnold et al. (2025) already present the repair model we use, and there are excellent recent papers that model repair and, in some cases, estimate it from data (Buckley et al. 2025; Ørsted et al. 2026; Faber et al. 2026, preprint). Understanding repair is an active research area about which we still know very little. We believe it is better to show how repair can be incorporated in a simple, illustrative form until more is known, which is what we do in the heat-injury predictions (Figure 6; Methods; Supplement Section 4). Any deeper dive into this is probably another paper as we are space limited. Additionally, we  already capture changes in interpretation when repair processes are accounted for by comparing predictions with and without repair. The specific values need empirical validation and this is not the purpose of our paper. As such, we have avoided a deep dive into repair.

6. Comparison with Alternative Frameworks. The paper does not discuss or compare the 4PL framework to recent mechanistic thermal tolerance models (e.g., dynamic energy budget models, or more recent machine-learning approaches for dose-response prediction). I’d recommend to add a brief section in the Discussion acknowledging the relationship to (or advantages over) complementary frameworks for thermal tolerance prediction. This would contextualize the 4PL's niche and limitations.

**Response**:

Pseudoreplication and Experimental Design Recommendations. While the paper identifies pseudoreplication as a problem with traditional approaches, practical guidance on experimental design to minimize it when using the 4PL is limited. The simulation section tests designs after the fact but does not proactively recommend optimal design. I would recommend to add a section (or expanded Methods discussion) recommending optimal temperature-duration grid designs, replication levels, and handling of nested random effects (e.g., vial-level variation). Use the simulation results to suggest minimal adequate designs for common taxa.

**Response**: We are not quite sure what reviewer 2 means by "does not proactivity recommend optimal design". We do. Simulations were not done after the fact, these are simulated scenarios to explore questions about how they perform for different experimental designs relative to a two-stage approach. 

To be honest, we cannot cover all aspects of experimental design in this study. We would argue that we have already done a very through set of simulations (as Reviewer 2 points out 29,000, across 29 different scenarios). That's a lot, even for a paper in the statistical literature. We believe it will be necessary for empiricists to do specific simulations for their experimental systems on a case-by case basis because it will be critical to inform the simulations with likely effect sizes and sample sizes relevant to those systems. 

Computational Requirements and Convergence Diagnostics. The paper provides no discussion of computational demands, convergence diagnostics (R-hat, effective sample size, divergence warnings), or potential convergence challenges users might encounter. I would recommend to include a table summarizing computational time (e.g., for a typical 4-species comparison on standard hardware), guidance on diagnosing non-convergence, and strategies for reparameterization if models fail to converge. This will reduce friction for new users.

**Response**: Good point. We now mention in each of our case studies exactly how much time (along with machine cores) each model took to run. Of course, `freqTLS` runs pretty instantaneously. In the supplement we also have lots on diagnostics etc, but we have been sure to make a bigger point through a targeted paragraph discussing these points for each case study. 

301-314. Case Study Coverage Balance. Three of the four case studies involve relatively well-behaved datasets (aphids, snow gum, vinegar fly). The zebrafish example 10 is noted to have a "sparse design," but only one case study explicitly uses a problematic design. I would recommend to add a brief supplementary case study (or extend zebrafish) demonstrating the 4PL's performance on truly minimal data (e.g., 2 temperatures × 3 durations, N=10 per cell), showing whether the method degrades gracefully or fails. This would clarify practical limits.

**Response**: This is a good idea, but we don't think this is necessary given that we already have fairly extensive simulations. We are not aware of any specific real datasets beyond these ones (and the zebrafish one) that are amendable to such design constraints. Of course, we could add a specific simulated case study but we believe this would be redundant with the simulations, and after all, it is only one realized dataset. Our simulations have 1000 simulated datasets. As such, we've opted to stick with what we have unless there is a specific case study Reviewer 2 has in mind.

394-410. Uncertainty Quantification in Field Predictions. Predictions of survival under field temperature regimes incorporate uncertainty via posterior draws, but the interpretation and use of credible intervals for decision-making (e.g., in conservation) is not discussed.

I would recommend to add guidance on how to interpret wide vs. narrow credible intervals in predictions, and how to translate them into risk assessments or management thresholds (e.g., "if lower 95% CI for survival falls below X%, apply intervention").

**Response**:

319-329. Sublethal Endpoints and Hurdle Models. The vinegar fly analysis includes a hurdle model separating reproductive failure from offspring-number changes, but this extension is mentioned only briefly and relegated to the supplement.
I would recommend to elevate one sublethal endpoint (e.g., heat coma or productivity) to the main text with full model specification and biological interpretation. This would demonstrate the framework's flexibility more compellingly.

**Response**: Thanks. Good suggestion. We didn't include it as one of the main examples because we wanted to show diversity of taxa and also a few case studies on how models can be used to calculate heat injury and survival with repair. However, we completely agree that this example would be a very useful addition. 

Code Availability and Reproducibility. The paper provides R packages but does not explicitly state whether raw data and analysis scripts for all four case studies are publicly available in a repository (GitHub, Zenodo, etc.). I would recommend to add a statement confirming (or clarifying conditions for) open access to scripts, data, and reproducible workflows (e.g., Rmarkdown documents) for each case study. This facilitates replication and community-driven extensions.

**Response**: We apologise that this was not clear. All data and code are public in the GitHub repository (https://github.com/daniel1noble/bayesTLS), which is both the `bayesTLS` package and the research compendium for the paper. The four case-study datasets ship with the package as documented data objects (`aphid_tdt`, `dsuzukii`, `snowgum_psii`, `zebrafish_o2`), with the raw files and build scripts in `data-raw/`. The full code for every case study is in `ms/supplement.qmd`, rendered with its code at https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/, and the manuscript figures and numbers come from `ms/ms.qmd`. The simulation is run by `scripts/simulations/run_simulations.R`. Stored model fits and simulation outputs are on OSF (https://osf.io/c6dxy) and can be downloaded with `make data` on terminal or bash, or just downloaded directly. We have expanded the Data and code availability statement in the manuscript to say all of this explicitly.

Minor Comments
233-25. Figure 4 presents complex multi-panel comparisons that would benefit from a more detailed caption explaining the distinction between "sparse" and "full" designs and the biological implications of bias at different replication levels.

**Response**: Great point. We have now added a new figure in the supplement (gridded experimental design) to help visualise the different simulated designs we explored so readers can better grasp what each simulated scenario pertains to making it clearer (hopefuly). We have also added a few sentences to point out, where things are biased, what it would mean for biological interpretations. 

The use of "relative" vs. "absolute" thresholds for CTmax is introduced conceptually but could be clarified earlier with a simple worked example in the Introduction.

**Response**: 

Summary Assessment
This is a substantive and well-executed paper that makes important methodological contributions to thermal ecology. The authors demonstrate rigor, acknowledge limitations candidly, and provide practical tools. The recommendations above are aimed at enhancing clarity, robustness, guidance, and practical utility rather than addressing fundamental flaws. Implementation of even a subset of these suggestions would further elevate the paper's impact and accessibility to practitioners.

**Response**: We would like to sincerely thank Reviewer 2 for their extremely thoughtful and constructive review. We are very happy they find the work rigorous, and that they think it will make an important methodological contribution to the field. We have made every attempt to try and take on board as many of the suggestions as possible. At times, some of these points were not easily accommodated within the word limits of the paper, and so, apologies if not all points were adequately addressed.
